title: Ulugh Beg and the Stars of Samarkand
paragraphs: In the early fifteenth century, Samarkand was one of the richest cities in the world. It was the capital of the empire founded by Amir Temur, and its markets, mosques and schools attracted scholars and artists from across Asia. In 1409, Temur's grandson, Mirzo Ulugh Beg, became governor of the city at the age of only fifteen. Unlike most rulers of his time, Ulugh Beg was more interested in science than in war, and he would use his position to turn Samarkand into a leading centre of learning.

Ulugh Beg's interest in astronomy is said to have begun when he visited the ruins of the Maragheh observatory in Persia as a child. As governor, he first built a madrasa, a school of higher education, in the Registan square, where mathematics and astronomy were taught alongside religion and philosophy. He invited some of the best scientists of the age to teach there, including the mathematician Jamshid al-Kashi and the astronomer Qadi Zada al-Rumi. Ulugh Beg himself took part in lessons and discussions.

In the 1420s, he ordered the construction of an observatory on a hill outside the city. The building was three storeys high and contained the largest instrument of its kind in the world at that time: a huge curved structure, known as a meridian arc, with a radius of about forty metres. Because of its size, astronomers could measure the positions of the sun, moon and stars with remarkable accuracy. Modern scholars believe that most of the observations were made without any form of magnification, as the telescope would not be invented for almost two centuries.

The most important result of the work at the observatory was the Zij-i-Sultani, a catalogue of 1,018 stars published in 1437. For each star, it gave a position that was more accurate than any previous catalogue, including the famous work of the Greek astronomer Ptolemy. The astronomers also calculated the length of the year as 365 days, 5 hours, 49 minutes and 15 seconds, which differs from the modern value by less than a minute. The catalogue was later translated into Latin and was used by European scientists for many years.

Ulugh Beg's interest in science did not protect him from the politics of his time. After the death of his father, Shah Rukh, in 1447, he became ruler of the whole empire, but his position was weak. Two years later, he was defeated by his own son, Abdullatif, and killed. Without his support, the scientists left Samarkand, and the observatory was gradually destroyed. Its stones were taken for other buildings, and within a few generations its exact location had been forgotten.

The observatory was rediscovered in 1908 by the Russian archaeologist Vasily Vyatkin, who found a document that described its position. Excavations revealed the lower part of the great meridian arc, which had been cut into the rock of the hill and had therefore survived. Today, the site is a museum and one of the most visited places in Samarkand. Ulugh Beg's name is remembered not only in Uzbekistan but also in space: a crater on the moon and a minor planet have been named after him.

questionGroups.instructions: Do the following statements agree with the information in the passage? Choose TRUE, FALSE or NOT GIVEN.

questions.explanation: Paragraph A: he became governor at the age of only fifteen.
questions.statement: Ulugh Beg became governor of Samarkand when he was a teenager.

questions.explanation: Paragraph B: mathematics and astronomy were taught alongside religion and philosophy.
questions.statement: Only religious subjects were taught at Ulugh Beg's madrasa.

questions.explanation: Paragraph C: the telescope would not be invented for almost two centuries.
questions.statement: The astronomers at the observatory used early telescopes.

questions.explanation: Paragraph D: positions were more accurate than any previous catalogue, including Ptolemy's.
questions.statement: The Zij-i-Sultani was more accurate than Ptolemy's catalogue.

questions.explanation: The passage says he found a document, but not how long he searched.
questions.statement: Vyatkin spent more than ten years searching for the observatory.

Paragraph D is about the star catalogue and its accuracy.
